title: Rupa's ocean of devotion's taste
hookLine: nobody reads an ocean front to back: a book of devotion built in waves
carry: rasa: devotion is something you taste
tomorrow: before the swim, a chart. what does devotion's map hold?
last: THE MISSING IS LOVE, HOLDING ON.

lines: NOBODY READS AN OCEAN FRONT TO BACK.
cards: Nobody reads an ocean front to back. You wade in, and the waves come to you. One Hindu book is built that way on purpose.
Its parts are called the eastern side, the southern, the western and the northern, and each side is divided into waves. Not chapters. Waves.
Rupa Goswami, who once sat by the rivers at Prayag learning about a seed and a creeper, has written a whole ocean. Why waves? Because of one word in the title.

teach.h: RASA: TASTE, THE FLAVOR OF A THING.
teach.b: Take the name a piece at a time. Bhakti, devotion. Rasa, taste, the flavor of a thing.
Amrita, nectar. Sindhu, ocean. The ocean of the nectar of devotion's taste.
The surprising word is rasa. Sanskrit poets and dramatists used it for the taste a scene leaves in its audience: the flavor of love, or grief, or wonder. Rupa borrows it for devotion.
So this isn't only a book about what a devotee should do.
It's about what devotion tastes like, and a taste comes in waves, not in steps. The first verse praises Krishna, in paraphrase, as the very form of the nectar of every taste.
The next bows to Chaitanya, by whose prompting in his heart, Rupa says, he writes at all. A neighbor tradition reaches for the same sense.
In the King James Bible, Psalm thirty-four says: “O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.”
Shared: faith as something tasted, known from the inside, not only learned about. And an honest difference. The psalm's taste is God's goodness, trusted in.
Rupa's rasa opens into a whole map of flavors, love as a servant, a friend, a parent, a beloved, with Krishna at the center of every one.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas study the Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu as a guide to devotional practice and feeling, alongside the Chaitanya Charitamrita.

games.q: what does “rupa goswami's bhakti rasamrita sindhu” mean?
o: a book on devotion as a taste, built like an ocean
a temple's rulebook for daily worship and its timing
a song cycle sung at a river festival every year

games.q: the title, a piece at a time — tap the pairs.
p: taste, the flavor of a thing

s: Rupa's book is mainly a rulebook of what devotees must do
its title calls it an ocean of devotion's taste: it's about what devotion tastes like.
the book's parts are called waves, not chapters
the eastern, southern, western and northern sides, each divided into waves.
Psalm 34 and Rupa's rasa say exactly the same thing
both speak of faith as tasted; the psalm tastes God's goodness, and Rupa maps devotion's flavors toward Krishna.

games.q: a classmate says, 'religions are all the same anyway. they all say taste and see.' what's the fair reply?
o: some things are shared, like faith as a taste, and some differ, like Rupa's map of love's flavors.
yes, they're all the same, so it doesn't matter which one.
no, they share nothing. each one stands completely alone.
games.why: Psalm 34 and Rupa both speak of tasting the holy. the psalm tastes God's goodness, trusted in; Rupa maps devotion's flavors, with Krishna at the center. alike in one way, honestly different in another.

practice: If there's something small to eat or drink near you, a sip of tea, a raisin, a piece of fruit, take it slowly and let the taste arrive like a wave: rising, full, then fading.
If there's nothing, notice the taste already in your mouth. Then rest at the shore, breathing.
